# Reverse a Singly Linked List

## Summary

Given the head of a singly linked list, reverse the direction of every `next`
pointer and return the new head. The nodes are re-linked in place; no new nodes
are allocated.

## Constraints

- The list may be empty (`head` is null).
- Values may repeat and may be negative.
- The reversal must be in place: `O(1)` extra space, no array copy.

## How the test cases are encoded

`tests/reverse-linked-list.json` stores each list as a plain array of values,
because a linked list has no natural JSON form. Build a list from `input[0]`,
reverse it, then flatten the result back to an array before comparing.

## Examples

| Input | Output | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `[1, 2, 3, 4]` | `[4, 3, 2, 1]` | the whole chain flips |
| `[1, 2, 1]` | `[1, 2, 1]` | palindromes look unchanged, but the pointers did move |
| `[7]` | `[7]` | a single node is its own reverse |
| `[]` | `[]` | null head stays null |

## Edge Cases

- Empty list — the loop body never runs and `prev` (null) is returned.
- Single node — `next` must end up null, not pointing at itself.
- Two nodes, the smallest case where the pointer dance is visible.
- Losing the rest of the list: if you overwrite `head.next` before saving it,
  everything after the current node is unreachable. That is *the* bug in this
  problem.

## Complexity

- **Time:** `O(n)` — one visit per node.
- **Space:** `O(1)` for the iterative version. The recursive version is also
  `O(n)` time but `O(n)` stack, which overflows on long lists.

## Why This Category

Linked-list problems are pointer-bookkeeping problems: the data never moves,
only the references. This one is the canonical drill for the three-pointer
pattern (`prev`, `current`, `next`) that also drives "reverse in k-groups",
"reorder list" and the merge step of a list merge sort.

## Thought Process

- Write the loop body in the order it must happen: save `next`, redirect
  `current.next` to `prev`, advance `prev`, advance `current`. Any other order
  drops the tail.
- Drawing three nodes and stepping through by hand is faster than reasoning
  about it abstractly — and it is what a debugger session is for.
- After the loop, `current` is null and `prev` is the new head. Returning
  `current` is the second most common mistake.
